Pichon’s room at the Quai d’Orsay, Paris, on Tuesday, September 30, 1919, at 10:30 a.m., included representatives from the United States, the British Empire, France, Italy, and Japan. The attendees were: Hon. F. L. Polk and Mr. L. Harrison from the United States; Sir Eyre Crowe and Mr. H. Norman from the British Empire; M. Clemenceau, M. Pichon, M. Dutasta, M. Berthelot, and M. de St. Quentin from France; M. Scialoja and Secretary M. Kawai from Italy; and M. Matsui from Japan. The joint secretariat included Captain Chapin from the United States, Captain Hinchley-Cooke from the British Empire, M. Massigli from France, and M. Zanchi from Italy, with M. Camerlynck as the interpreter. Additional individuals present for specific matters included Rear Admiral McCully, Colonel Logan, Colonel Browning, Major Tyler, and Mr. E. L. Dresel from the United States; General Sackville-West, Lt.-Col. Kisch, Mr. McFadyean, Mr. Ibbetson-James, Mr. Forbes-Adam, and Mr. Bourdil from the British Empire. The meeting addressed the definition of 'upkeep of the troops of occupation' as specified in Article 9 of the Armistice Convention of November 11, 1918, which states that the upkeep of the troops of occupation in the Rhenish territories is at the charge of the German Government. A sub-Commission at Spa defined 'upkeep' as including expenditures for the daily life of occupying troops, maintenance of fixed effective forces, and readiness to resist aggression or resume hostilities. The sub-Commission determined daily maintenance costs per army: French Army at 16.60 francs, Belgian Army at 16.13 francs, British Army at 17.06 francs, and American Army at 31.14 francs. The total monthly expenditure was evaluated at slightly over 600,000,000 francs. The United States objected to the use of the French daily rate as a base for calculating expenses, citing that the American Army's average daily upkeep was higher than that of other armies. General Pershing had previously stated in a letter to Marshal Foch on March 8, 1919, that the United States could not accept the French rate as a basis for estimating German obligations. The French and Belgian delegations supported the use of a general average rate based on the French army's rate, while the Italian military representative expressed a preference for a similar approach. The United States emphasized that it had the right to demand full reimbursement of its army's occupation expenses from Germany, and noted that it was beginning to replace conscripted troops with volunteer troops from its regular army. The meeting also discussed the need for a unified standard in the valuation of maintenance expenses, with the understanding that if Germany could not pay in full, payments would be made as partial advances to be deducted from total periodic payments, not as complete liquidation of expenditures. The decision was made to adopt a single daily price for all armies, with the French rate being accepted as the standard. The British representative noted that the proposed rate was valid only if all armies accepted the French daily rate, which had not been accepted by General Pershing. The French delegate shared the Belgian view that differences in army costs were of little importance, and that the key issue was the reimbursement of deficits created by occupation expenses. The United States argued that it should not bear the cost of its occupation expenses when Germany was responsible under the Armistice terms. The meeting also addressed the issue of the Aaland Islands, which was adjourned. The Baltic Commission's report dated August 25, 1919, on Karelia and Petchenga was discussed, with Mr. Kammerer noting that the Commission had not made any proposals to the Council. Mr. Clemenceau responded that Finland's desires might be considered, but no formal proposal had been made. The meeting concluded with the decision to communicate the minutes of the Commission on Inquiry at Smyrna to the Greek representative and to allow the Greek representative to notify the Commission of any complaints. The matter of the blockade of Soviet Russia was adjourned pending a response from the Swedish Government. The Supreme Economic Council was instructed to examine German demands for supplies and raw materials under Article 235 of the Peace Treaty, with programs and purchase orders to be reviewed by the Committee on Raw Materials and the Consultative Provisioning Committee to prevent speculation and unjustified increases in prices. The meeting also noted that the post-war economic situation had caused a break in monetary relations, with disparities in national currency values increasing due to unstable exchange rates, and that the well-being and security of Europe were interdependent, requiring collective efforts for reconstruction.

answer_text: Goodenow reported on the international tonnage commission's final report, which was transmitted from the Levant Herald and dated December 18, 1873. The report, abridged and received on March 18, 1874, outlined the commission's decision to adopt the Moorsom system of measurement—100 English cubic feet or 283 cubic meters—as the unit of net tonnage for ships. The commission determined that deductions from gross tonnage to determine net tonnage should not exceed 5 percent, covering crew accommodations, officer cabins, crew privies, and covered or inclosed deck spaces. For steamships, specific deductions were made for engine and boiler rooms, shaft tunnels, and fixed coal-bunkers. If coal was stored only in movable bulk-heads or side bunkers, the rules of the Lower Danube applied, with allowances of 50 percent for paddle-wheeled ships and 75 percent for screw ships. The report also proposed a compromise on tolls for the Suez Canal, with an extra toll of 4 francs per net ton for ships whose engine deductions followed the English merchant shipping act of 1854, reduced to 3 francs for ships that noted the recommended net tonnage system. This extra toll would decrease by half a franc per ton for every 100,000-ton increase in annual tonnage, reaching a definitive suppression at 2,600,000 tons, after which the toll would be 10 francs per net ton. Ships of war, troop transports, and those in ballast were exempted. This report was communicated to Mr. Fish on March 18, 1874, and formed the basis of Goodenow’s initial argument regarding maritime tonnage and Suez Canal dues. Between March 18 and April 23, 1874, Goodenow expanded his report to include a financial assessment of the Ottoman Empire, transmitted on April 23, 1874. The report, authored by Thomas C. Bruce, a member of the Imperial Ottoman Bank and a former Parliament member, estimated the annual revenue of Turkey at 24,800,000 Turkish liras (equivalent to 24,800,000 pounds at 18 shillings per lira). The Sultan receives approximately 1,800,000 pounds annually as his civil-list allowance, though the actual expenditure of the imperial court is not officially reported but is said to be around £4,500,000 annually. The commission found that the government's temporary liabilities, including arrears and interest on advances from 1873, totaled 14,725,274 pounds Turkish. The government has bonds of 7,385,000 pounds from the 1873 loan and 255,000 pounds from the railway loan, but the latter is restricted to railway works and thus cannot be used for floating debt. Additionally, 7,085,270 pounds Turkish in tax arrears are due to the treasury, but their encashment is uncertain and thus not a reliable immediate resource. The commission concluded that retrenchment must begin at the head of government to restore credit and enable liquidation of floating debt at reasonable rates. This would require painful sacrifices, including the reorganization of regular services and the deferral of many improvement projects such as land and sea communications, mining, and port development. The commission emphasized that the financial system could be improved, and that with proper management, Turkey could surpass the financial standing of Spain. The report was signed by multiple officials, including Yussuf Bey, Edib Effendi, Ohannes Tchamitch Effendi, and members of the Imperial Ottoman Bank, and was dated February 17, 1874. The financial analysis was based on a detailed examination of revenue and expenditure, with the commission noting that the old taxes showed elasticity, with the sheep-tax increasing from 900,000 to 2,000,000 pounds Turkish, and that the tithe on agricultural produce varied with harvests. The customs revenue was found to be undercollected, and the government's renunciation of commercial treaties with foreign powers was seen as a positive step. The tobacco tax, though currently under-estimated, was recommended to be temporarily reduced by 500,000 pounds Turkish, with the expectation that future collection would yield greater results due to the universal use of Turkish tobacco and its high international demand. The new stamp duties were also expected to yield more than estimated, given the historical elasticity of revenue. The commission accepted the budgeted expenditure figures as presented, noting that the administration of mines and forests had high expenditures relative to receipts, but that these were justified by future development plans. The railway guarantees were expected to decrease over time as the railways began to generate profits. The commission concluded that with proper management, an equilibrium between revenue and expenditure could be achieved, and that the floating debt, which was the primary obstacle to financial credibility, must be addressed through assurance of repayment and the prevention of renewal. Without such assurance, the government's credit would not be restored. The report emphasized that the financial system could be restructured to place Turkey on a more solid basis than any other European country except England and Germany.
